abstract: Terahertz frequencies are expected to become a key player in next-generation wireless communications. For this transition to occur seamlessly, tunable bandpass filters for channel selection are essential. However, conventional Fabry-Pérot cavity-based bandpass filters face inherent limitations. Specifically, their tunability is restricted by physical constraints, such as the maximum achievable mirror separation. In this work, drawing inspiration from electronic interferometers, we demonstrate a continuously tunable bandpass filter operating near 0.3 THz by exploiting the geometric phase of light, the Pancharatnam-Berry phase. Our device incorporates intracavity waveplates for polarization control and is described by a mathematical expression analogous to that of the electronic interferometer governed by the Aharonov-Bohm phase, thereby realizing a photonic analogue. Using custom-designed subwavelength waveplates and cavity mirrors, we achieve a finesse of $\mathcal{F}\approx17$, a quality factor of $Q\approx1.5\times10^{3}$, and a resonance linewidth of $Δf_{\mathrm{FWHM}}\approx 200$ MHz. Beyond terahertz communication technology, this system is expected to find applications in fields requiring high frequency resolution, such as spectroscopy.
